final_proof:
Let \(v_p\) denote the usual \(p\)-adic valuation on \(\mathbb Q\), and let \(|x|_p=p^{-v_p(x)}\) for \(x\ne0\), with \(|0|_p=0\). Recall that \(\mathbb Q_p\) is the completion of \(\mathbb Q\) for this absolute value and that the ultrametric inequality
\[
|x+y|_p\leq\max\{|x|_p,|y|_p\}
\]
holds. We construct an injection into \(\mathbb Q_p\) from the set of all infinite binary sequences.

Let \(B=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\), where \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). For \(a=(a_0,a_1,\ldots)\in B\), consider the partial sums
\[
S_N(a)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}a_np^n.
\]
If \(M>N\), the ultrametric inequality gives
\[
|S_M(a)-S_N(a)|_p
=\left|\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}a_np^n\right|_p
\leq p^{-(N+1)}.
\]
Indeed, every nonzero summand has absolute value \(|p^n|_p=p^{-n}\leq p^{-(N+1)}\). Hence \((S_N(a))\) is Cauchy and therefore has a limit in \(\mathbb Q_p\). Define
\[
\Phi(a)=\lim_{N\to\infty}S_N(a)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_np^n.
\]

We show that \(\Phi\) is injective. Let \(a,b\in B\) be distinct, and let \(k\) be the least index for which \(a_k\ne b_k\). Then
\[
\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)=(a_k-b_k)p^k+R,
\qquad
R=\sum_{n=k+1}^{\infty}(a_n-b_n)p^n.
\]
Every finite partial sum defining \(R\) has \(p\)-adic absolute value at most \(p^{-(k+1)}\), again by the ultrametric inequality. Since the closed ball
\[
\{x\in\mathbb Q_p:|x|_p\leq p^{-(k+1)}\}
\]
is closed, passage to the limit yields
\[
|R|_p\leq p^{-(k+1)}<p^{-k}.
\]
On the other hand, \(a_k-b_k=\pm1\), and consequently
\[
|(a_k-b_k)p^k|_p=p^{-k}.
\]
If a non-Archimedean absolute value satisfies \(|x|>|y|\), then \(|x+y|=|x|\): the ultrametric inequality gives \(|x+y|\leq|x|\), while
\[
|x|=|(x+y)-y|\leq\max\{|x+y|,|y|\}
\]
forces \(|x+y|\geq|x|\). Applying this with \(x=(a_k-b_k)p^k\) and \(y=R\), we obtain
\[
|\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)|_p=p^{-k}>0.
\]
Thus \(\Phi(a)\ne\Phi(b)\), proving that \(\Phi\) is injective.

It remains to show that \(B\) is uncountable. If its elements could be listed as
\[
b^{(0)},b^{(1)},b^{(2)},\ldots,
\]
define a binary sequence \(c\) by \(c_n=1-b^{(n)}_n\). For every \(n\), the sequence \(c\) differs from \(b^{(n)}\) in its \(n\)-th coordinate, so \(c\) is absent from the purported list, a contradiction. Therefore \(B\) is uncountable. Since the uncountable set \(B\) injects into \(\mathbb Q_p\), the set \(\mathbb Q_p\) is uncountable.
